title: Smooth rational models and finite-stage lifting of regular maps
statement:
Let $X$ be an affine scheme that is a finite disjoint union of generically reduced schemes (reduced [def-pc-reduced-scheme] at every generic point) of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] over fields of characteristic zero; the fields need not be the same. Then there is a small nonempty directed set $I$ and an inverse system $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ of generically reduced affine finite-type $\mathbf Q$-schemes, with smooth [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] affine transition morphisms $X_j\to X_i$ for $j\ge i$, whose limit in schemes is $X$. Every projection $p_i:X\to X_i$ is regular [def-per-regular-scheme-morphism] (flat with geometrically regular fibres). One may choose the projections schematically dominant. Empty schemes are allowed, and finite disjoint unions admit such presentations as well.

The following finite-stage comparison holds for ANY two inverse systems of affine finite-type $\mathbf Q$-schemes with smooth affine transitions and Noetherian limits $X=\varprojlim_{i\in I}X_i$ and $Y=\varprojlim_{j\in J}Y_j$. If $h:Y\to X$ is a regular scheme morphism, then for every $i\in I$ and every $j_0\in J$ there are $j\ge j_0$ and a SMOOTH morphism $h_{ji}:Y_j\to X_i$ such that $p_i h=h_{ji}q_j$, where $p_i,q_j$ are the limit projections. In particular this applies to the identity of one scheme equipped with two different presentations. No compatibility of $h$ with choices of characteristic-zero ground fields is assumed. The comparison is an assertion about finite-stage scheme morphisms, not about desingularization towers.

source.place: Definition 7.2; proof of Theorem 7.4, the two finite-stage factorizations through the smooth locus; Theorem 7.5 and its schematic-image refinement, pp.18--21; https://arxiv.org/pdf/0905.3580 (arXiv:0905.3580v1), WANTED archival copy

proof.text: First treat $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$ of finite type over one characteristic-zero field $k$. Since a field is Noetherian (its only ideals are zero and itself), the cited finite-type and finite-presentation lemmas give $A=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_m)$. Let $R_0\subset k$ be the finitely generated rational subalgebra generated by the coefficients of these finitely many polynomials and put $B_0=R_0[x]/(f)$. The maps sending each coefficient and variable to itself give mutually inverse maps $k\otimes_{R_0}B_0\simeq A$ by the tensor pushout property. Generic flatness gives $a\ne0$ in $R_0$ with $(B_0)_a$ flat over $R_0$; the localization flatness lemma makes it flat over $(R_0)_a$. Replace $R_0,B_0$ by these localizations, which remain finite type over $\mathbf Q$ and still give $A$. Thus $R_0\subset k$ is a domain and $B_0$ is flat over it.

source.place: 051T generic flatness; 00FP finite presentation; coefficient presentation argument

proof.text: Let $I$ consist of all finitely generated rational subalgebras $C\subset k$ containing $R_0$, ordered by $C\preceq D$ when $C\subseteq D$ and $C\to D$ is smooth. This is a small set (a subset of the power set of $k$), nonempty since it contains $R_0$. Identity maps are smooth directly from the lifting definition, smooth composition gives transitivity, and antisymmetry follows from inclusion. Here is the finite refinement argument, not a separate lemma: for $C_1,C_2\in I$ and finite $F\subset k$, let $S\subset k$ be the algebra generated by $C_1,C_2,F$. Each $C_t\hookrightarrow S$ is injective and finite type between domains; its fraction-field extension is separable because it has characteristic zero. Generic smoothness yields $g_t\ne0$ in $S$ with $C_t\to S_{g_t}$ smooth. Then $D=S_{g_1g_2}\subset k$ is smooth over both $C_t$, by further principal localization, and contains $F$. Hence $I$ is directed, and its underlying subrings cover $k$.

source.place: 07ND generic smoothness for domains; finite simultaneous localization argument

proof.text: Put $B_C=C\otimes_{R_0}B_0$ and $X_C=\operatorname{Spec}B_C$. Every $B_C$ is a finite type rational algebra, hence Noetherian; it is flat over $C$ by flat base change. Apply [lem-per-flat-model-generic-reducedness] with $R=R_0,D=C,B=B_0$ and the given embedding into $k$: its field base change is exactly the generically reduced ring $A$, so $B_C$ is generically reduced. For $C\preceq D$, the identification $B_D=D\otimes_C B_C$, obtained by sending pure tensors to pure tensors in both directions, identifies $B_C\to B_D$ with a base change of the smooth map $C\to D$. Thus $X_D\to X_C$ is smooth and affine.

source.place: 00HS and 030V, flat generic reducedness; smooth base change

proof.text: The compatible maps $B_C\to A$ exhibit $A$ as their colimit: compatible ring maps from all $B_C$ to a ring $T$ restrict to one map $k\to T$, because the subrings $C$ cover $k$ and every finite collection is contained in an upper stage; together with the common map $B_0\to T$ the tensor pushout property gives a unique map $k\otimes_{R_0}B_0\to T$. The affine limit lemma therefore identifies $X$ with $\varprojlim X_C$. Moreover, tensoring each inclusion $C\hookrightarrow k$ with the flat $R_0$-module $B_0$ gives an injection $B_C\hookrightarrow A$. On affine schemes schematic dominance means precisely this injection: the kernel sheaf of $\mathcal O_{X_C}\to(p_C)_*\mathcal O_X$ is the sheaf associated to the kernel of $B_C\to A$, which is zero. This proves the optional dominance without a schematic-image replacement.

source.place: tensor pushout property; affine limits (Limits Tag 01YW); flat tensor injection

proof.text: We record explicitly the affine ring/scheme translation used below. For $R\to T$ with $T$ Noetherian, every fibre $T\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ is a localization of $T/\mathfrak pT$, hence Noetherian: ideals of a quotient lift to finitely generated ideals, and localization preserves Noetherianity. The affine fibre-product identification and the affine flatness criterion identify flatness and fibres on the two sides. A regular ring map thus gives a regular scheme morphism, since the cited geometrically-regular extension lemma tests every finite residue-field extension, not just purely inseparable ones. Conversely a regular scheme morphism tests all finite extensions and in particular the purely inseparable ones; regularity of its affine fibres says exactly that the fibre rings are regular. Thus the two meanings of regular coincide here.

source.place: 0382 geometric regularity and 07BZ regular homomorphisms; affine dictionary

proof.text: For fixed $C$, the tail $D\succeq C$ is small nonempty filtered, has the same colimit $A$ (any stage has a common upper stage with $C$), and each $B_C\to B_D$ is smooth. All fibres of $B_C\to A$ are Noetherian by step 5 because $A$ is Noetherian. Apply the smooth-colimit regularity lemma and step 5 to obtain regularity of every $p_C$. The same argument proves that every projection of ANY directed inverse system of affine finite-type rational schemes with smooth transitions and Noetherian limit is regular; no injectivity of its transition ring maps is needed.

For finitely many field components use the product of their nonempty directed index sets, and at each stage the finite disjoint union of the corresponding models. A finite disjoint union of affine schemes is affine with coordinate ring the finite product: the standard orthogonal idempotents split its spectrum into precisely the component spectra. The resulting ring colimit is the finite product of the component colimits, since representatives and all finitely many equalities can be moved to one common tuple of upper indices. Hence the affine limit is the required disjoint union. Smoothness, generic reducedness, schematic dominance and regularity are checked separately on these open-and-closed components, using the stalk/fibre definitions (and componentwise injectivity for dominance). For the empty scheme take the constant empty system over a singleton. This also treats any empty components.

source.place: finite componentwise assembly of the preceding construction

proof.text: Now take the two arbitrary presentations in the comparison assertion. Write $A_i=\Gamma(X_i,\mathcal O)$, $B_j=\Gamma(Y_j,\mathcal O)$, $A=\Gamma(X,\mathcal O)$ and $B=\Gamma(Y,\mathcal O)$. The affine limit lemma identifies their ring colimits with $A,B$. Every morphism between rational schemes respects their rational structure maps: a unital ring map fixes integers and inverses of nonzero integers. The finite rational algebra $A_i$ is finitely presented since $\mathbf Q$ is Noetherian. Finite-presentation factorization applied to $A_i\to A\to B=\varinjlim B_j$ gives $A_i\to B_{j_1}$. Choose a common upper bound $j\ge j_1,j_0$; compose to obtain $g:Y_j\to X_i$ with $gq_j=p_i h$. At this point $g$ is only finite type: a finite set of rational algebra generators of $B_j$ also generates it as an $A_i$-algebra.

source.place: finite-presentation factorization through a filtered colimit; BMT proof of Theorem 7.4 first factorization

proof.text: By step 6 the projection $X\to X_i$ is regular. By hypothesis $h$ is regular. Translate them to ring maps by step 5, and apply regular composition to $A_i\to A\to B$: every composite fibre is Noetherian because it is a quotient followed by a localization of the Noetherian ring $B$. For $y\in Y$, put $z=q_j(y)$, $x=g(z)$. The local criterion for regular maps gives regularity of $\mathcal O_{X_i,x}\to\mathcal O_{Y,y}$ and of $\mathcal O_{Y_j,z}\to\mathcal O_{Y,y}$, the latter from regularity of $q_j$. This latter map is flat and local, hence faithfully flat and surjective on spectra. Regular permanence for the local triangle therefore proves that $\mathcal O_{X_i,x}\to\mathcal O_{Y_j,z}$ is regular. Notice that this conclusion is asserted only at points in the image of $Y$.

source.place: 07QI regular composition; 07C0 local criterion; 07NT regular permanence; BMT Theorem 7.4

proof.text: This makes $g$ smooth at $z$. Indeed let $P\subset A_i,Q\subset B_j$ correspond to $x,z$, and $F=B_j\otimes_{A_i}\kappa(P)$ with prime $Q_F$ over $Q$. The fibre-local-ring isomorphism identifies $F_{Q_F}$ with $(B_j)_Q/P(B_j)_Q$, which is regular local by regularity of $(A_i)_P\to(B_j)_Q$. The finite type $\kappa(P)$-algebra $F$ has separable residue extension at $Q_F$, since its fields have characteristic zero. The regular-local/separable-residue smoothness criterion gives smoothness of $\kappa(P)\to F$ there. The flat-smooth-fibre criterion now applies: $A_i\to B_j$ is finitely presented by the Noetherian finite-type lemma (take its element $g=1$), and its local map at $Q$ is flat because it is regular. Thus $A_i\to B_j$ is smooth at $Q$.

source.place: 00TV regular local ring and separable residue criterion; 01V9 smooth-at-point criterion

proof.text: Let $U\subset Y_j$ be the smooth locus of $g$, the union of the principal opens specified by the singular-ideal node. Step 10 gives $q_j(Y)\subset U$. Write its closed complement as $Z=\operatorname{Spec}(B_j/H_{B_j/A_i})$. On the directed tail $k\ge j$, form $Z_k=Y_k\times_{Y_j}Z$, affine and quasi-compact. Their limit is empty: on rings it is $B\otimes_{B_j}(B_j/H)=B/HB$, by the tensor pushout property and the colimit universal property; its spectrum is the inverse image of $Z$, which has no points. By the nonempty-limit lemma, not all $Z_k$ can be nonempty. Choose $k\ge j$ with $Z_k$ empty. Thus the transition $Y_k\to Y_j$ has image inside $U$ and factors uniquely through it. This argument includes $Y$ empty and does not assume that the limit projection is surjective.

source.place: singular ideal Definition 07C5; Limits 01Z2; BMT Theorem 7.4 second factorization

proof.text: The transition $Y_k\to Y_j$ is smooth by assumption, so its factor $Y_k\to U$ is smooth by restriction to an open target. By construction $g|_U:U\to X_i$ is smooth: its principal open cover consists of smooth rational algebra maps. Their composite $h_{ki}:Y_k\to U\to X_i$ is smooth, using composition on affine charts. The defining factorization and transition equations give $h_{ki}q_k=gq_j=p_i h$, and $k\ge j_0$. Finally take $h=\mathrm{id}$ to obtain the assertion about two presentations; identities are flat and their fibres and finite field base changes are spectra of fields, so they are regular. All uses of rational coefficients above come from the unique rational structure map, with no compatibility between the original ground fields required.

source.place: smooth restriction and composition; conclusion of BMT Theorem 7.4
